questions.q: a and b are rational numbers and a + b√2 = (1 + √2)². What is a + b?
questions.x: (1 + √2)² = 1 + 2√2 + 2 = 3 + 2√2. Since √2 is irrational, the rational parts and the √2 parts must match: a = 3, b = 2, so a + b = 5. Dropping the middle term 2√2 gives 3.

questions.q: A = {1, 2} and B = {2, 3}. What is (A × B) ∩ (B × A)?
questions.x: A × B = {(1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 2), (2, 3)} and B × A = {(2, 1), (2, 2), (3, 1), (3, 2)}. Only (2, 2) is in both. Order matters in a pair, so (2, 3) and (3, 2) are different elements.

questions.q: f(x) = ax³ + bx + 5, and f(−2) = 3. What is f(2)?
questions.x: g(x) = ax³ + bx is odd. f(−2) = g(−2) + 5 = 3 gives g(−2) = −2, so g(2) = 2 and f(2) = 2 + 5 = 7. Treating f itself as odd gives −3.

questions.q: a, b and c are positive numbers other than 1, and aˣ = bʸ = cᶻ with x, y, z non-zero. If b² = ac, which relation holds?
questions.x: Let aˣ = bʸ = cᶻ = k (k ≠ 1), so log a = (log k)/x, log b = (log k)/y, log c = (log k)/z. b² = ac gives 2 log b = log a + log c, so 2/y = 1/x + 1/z. Check a = 2, b = 4, c = 8, k = 64: x = 6, y = 3, z = 2 and 2/3 = 1/6 + 1/2.

questions.q: On which set is f(x) = 1/√(x − 1) + 1/(x − 3) continuous?
questions.x: 1/√(x − 1) needs x − 1 > 0, i.e. x > 1, and 1/(x − 3) needs x ≠ 3. On (1, 3) ∪ (3, ∞) both terms are continuous, so f is; at x = 1 and x = 3 f is not even defined.

questions.q: For every square matrix A, the matrix A + Aᵗ is:
questions.x: (A + Aᵗ)ᵗ = Aᵗ + (Aᵗ)ᵗ = Aᵗ + A, so A + Aᵗ is symmetric. It is A − Aᵗ that is skew-symmetric. A = I gives 2I, which is not singular, and A = [[1, 1], [0, 1]] gives [[2, 1], [1, 2]], which is not diagonal.

questions.q: The two roots of x² − 8x + k = 0 differ by 2. What is the value of k?
questions.x: (α − β)² = (α + β)² − 4αβ, so 4 = 64 − 4k and k = 15. Check: α + β = 8 and α − β = 2 give roots 5 and 3, product 15. k = 16 would make the roots equal.

questions.q: ω is a complex cube root of unity. What is the least positive integer n for which (1 + ω²)ⁿ = (1 + ω⁴)ⁿ?
questions.x: 1 + ω² = −ω and 1 + ω⁴ = 1 + ω = −ω². So (−ω)ⁿ = (−ω²)ⁿ means ωⁿ = ω²ⁿ, i.e. ωⁿ = 1, so n is a multiple of 3. Check n = 3: (−ω)³ = −1 and (−ω²)³ = −ω⁶ = −1; n = 1 and n = 2 give −ω ≠ −ω² and ω² ≠ ω.

questions.q: If (3x + 5)/((x + 1)(x + 3)) = A/(x + 1) + B/(x + 3), what is the value of B?
questions.x: 3x + 5 = A(x + 3) + B(x + 1). Put x = −3: −4 = −2B, so B = 2. Check: x = −1 gives 2 = 2A, A = 1, and A + B = 3 matches the x coefficient. Dropping the minus sign on −4 gives −2.

questions.q: Sana spends Rs. 600 on mangoes at Rs. 200 per kg, and another Rs. 600 on mangoes at Rs. 300 per kg. What is her average price per kg?
questions.x: Equal amounts of money at two prices give the harmonic mean of the prices: 2 × 200 × 300/(200 + 300) = 240. Check: she buys 3 kg + 2 kg = 5 kg for Rs. 1200, i.e. Rs. 240 per kg. The arithmetic mean 250 is the usual slip.

questions.q: The letters of the word MULTAN are arranged so that every arrangement begins with M and ends with N. How many such arrangements are there?
questions.x: M and N are fixed at the ends, so only the middle four letters U, L, T, A are arranged: 4! = 24. Fixing only one end gives 5! = 120, and no restriction gives 6! = 720.

questions.q: For every integer n ≥ 2, the product (1 − 1/2²)(1 − 1/3²)(1 − 1/4²) … (1 − 1/n²) equals:
questions.x: For n = 2 the product is 3/4, and (n + 1)/(2n) = 3/4; for n = 3 it is 3/4 × 8/9 = 2/3 = 4/6. Inductive step: (k + 1)/(2k) × (k² + 2k)/(k + 1)² = (k + 2)/(2(k + 1)). The other forms give 1/4, 3/2 and 1 at n = 2.

questions.q: In the principle of mathematical induction, P(m) is shown true and P(k) ⇒ P(k + 1) is shown for every integer k ≥ m. Then P(n) is proved true for:
o: only n = m and n = m + 1
questions.x: P(m) starts the chain and the inductive step carries it from each k to k + 1, so it reaches every integer from m upward. Nothing is proved for integers below m, so 'every positive integer' is wrong when m > 1.

questions.q: What is the value of tan 75° − tan 15°?
questions.x: tan 75° = tan(45° + 30°) = 2 + √3 and tan 15° = tan(45° − 30°) = 2 − √3, so the difference is 2√3. Adding them instead gives 4.

questions.q: For every x, sin 3x cos x − cos 3x sin x equals:
questions.x: This is sin(A − B) with A = 3x and B = x, so it equals sin 2x. sin 4x would come from sin(A + B), which has a plus sign.

questions.q: What is the smallest positive period of y = sin²x?
questions.x: sin²x = (1 − cos 2x)/2, and cos 2x has period 2π/2 = π. Also sin²(x + π) = (−sin x)² = sin²x, while π/2 fails (sin²0 = 0 but sin²(π/2) = 1). 2π is a period but not the smallest.

questions.q: In triangle ABC, a = 13, b = 14 and c = 15. What is tan(A/2)?
Which of these graphs is defined for every real number x?
questions.x: tan x takes every real value on (−π/2, π/2), so tan⁻¹x has domain all real x. sin⁻¹x and cos⁻¹x need −1 ≤ x ≤ 1, and sec⁻¹x needs |x| ≥ 1.

questions.q: The general solution of cos θ = 1/√2 is (n ∈ Z):
questions.x: The principal value is π/4 and cos is even with period 2π, so θ = 2nπ ± π/4. θ = nπ ± π/4 would also include 3π/4, where cos θ = −1/√2.

questions.q: At the origin, the curve y = ∛x has:
o: a corner, with different one-sided slopes
questions.x: [∛h − 0]/h = h^(−2/3), which grows without bound as h → 0 from either side, so the tangent at (0, 0) is vertical (the y-axis). The curve is smooth there, so it is not a corner.

questions.q: Here x is measured in degrees. What is d/dx sin(x°)?
questions.x: x° = πx/180 radians, so sin(x°) = sin(πx/180) and the chain rule gives (π/180) cos(πx/180) = (π/180) cos(x°). The rule (sin x)′ = cos x holds only for x in radians.

questions.q: ∫ (eˣ + e⁻ˣ)² dx equals:
questions.x: (eˣ + e⁻ˣ)² = e^(2x) + 2 + e^(−2x), which integrates to ½e^(2x) + 2x − ½e^(−2x) + C. The sign of the last term comes from the factor −2 in the exponent; forgetting the middle term 2 drops the 2x.

questions.q: A particle moves along a line with velocity v = 3t² − 2t m/s. At t = 0 its position is s = 4 m. What is its position at t = 2 s?
questions.x: s = ∫ v dt = t³ − t² + C, and s(0) = 4 gives C = 4. Then s(2) = 8 − 4 + 4 = 8 m. Leaving out the constant gives 4 m.

questions.q: y = sin 2x is a solution of which differential equation?
questions.x: y′ = 2 cos 2x and y″ = −4 sin 2x = −4y, so y″ + 4y = 0. Using the factor 2 instead of 2² gives y″ + 2y = 0.

questions.q: What are the points of trisection of the segment joining (−3, 6) and (6, −3)?
questions.x: They divide the segment in the ratios 1 : 2 and 2 : 1: ((−6 + 6)/3, (12 − 3)/3) = (0, 3) and ((−3 + 12)/3, (6 − 6)/3) = (3, 0). (1.5, 1.5) is the midpoint, not a trisection point.

questions.q: What is the perpendicular distance from the point (x₁, y₁) to the line ax + by + c = 0?
questions.x: Substitute the point into the left side, take the absolute value and divide by √(a² + b²). Example: from (0, 0) to 3x + 4y − 10 = 0 the distance is 10/5 = 2.

questions.q: Eliminating θ from x = 3 sec θ, y = 2 tan θ gives which curve?
questions.x: sec²θ − tan²θ = 1 gives x²/9 − y²/4 = 1, a hyperbola. Adding the squares by mistake gives the ellipse x²/9 + y²/4 = 1.

questions.q: The tangent to the curve xy = 8 at (2, 4) meets the x-axis at A and the y-axis at B. What is the area of triangle OAB, where O is the origin?
questions.x: y = 8/x gives y′ = −8/x² = −2 at x = 2. The tangent y − 4 = −2(x − 2), i.e. y = −2x + 8, meets the axes at (4, 0) and (0, 8), so the area is ½ × 4 × 8 = 16.

questions.q: What is i × (i × j)?
questions.x: i × j = k, and then i × k = −j. Taking i × k = j (wrong cyclic order) gives j.

questions.q: A plot of land is 40 m long. Its widths, measured every 10 m along its length, are 0, 12, 16, 14 and 0 m. Using the trapezium rule, what is its area?
questions.x: h = 10, so area ≈ (10/2)[0 + 0 + 2(12 + 16 + 14)] = 5 × 84 = 420 m². Forgetting the factor ½ gives 840 m².

questions.q: A pressure is given as 5 N cm⁻². In pascals (N m⁻²) this is:
questions.x: 1 cm² = 10⁻⁴ m², so 5 N cm⁻² = 5 N / 10⁻⁴ m² = 5 × 10⁴ Pa. Converting cm to m without squaring gives 5 × 10² Pa; multiplying by 10⁻⁴ instead of dividing gives 5 × 10⁻⁴ Pa.

questions.q: A uniform metre rule of weight 2 N is pivoted at its 30 cm mark. A weight hung at the 10 cm mark keeps it horizontal. This weight is:
questions.x: The rule's weight acts at 50 cm, 0.2 m from the pivot: 2 × 0.2 = 0.4 N m. The hung weight is also 0.2 m from the pivot, so W × 0.2 = 0.4 and W = 2 N. Measuring its arm from the 0 cm end instead of the pivot gives the wrong values.

questions.q: Torque plays the same role in rotational motion as which quantity does in linear motion?
questions.x: A net force produces linear acceleration; a net torque produces angular acceleration, so torque is the rotational analogue of force. Mass corresponds to moment of inertia, momentum to angular momentum.

questions.q: Trolleys of mass 1 kg and 3 kg are held together at rest with a compressed spring between them, then released on a smooth floor. The ratio of their kinetic energies (1 kg trolley : 3 kg trolley) just after separation is:
questions.x: Total momentum stays zero, so both trolleys have equal momentum p. K = p²/2m, so K ∝ 1/m and the ratio is 3 : 1. Check with speeds: 1 kg at 3v, 3 kg at v: ½(1)(9v²) : ½(3)(v²) = 9 : 3 = 3 : 1. 9 : 1 is the ratio of the squared speeds alone.

questions.q: A 10 g bullet moving horizontally at 300 m s⁻¹ embeds itself in a 0.99 kg wooden block hanging at rest from long strings. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², the block with the bullet swings up to a height of:
questions.x: Momentum: 0.01 × 300 = (0.01 + 0.99)V, so V = 3 m s⁻¹. Then ½V² = gh gives h = 9/20 = 0.45 m. Kinetic energy is not conserved in the impact, only during the swing. Forgetting the ½ gives 0.9 m.

questions.q: A 1 kg ball is dropped from a height of 20 m. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s⁻², its speed at the point where its kinetic energy equals its potential energy (measured from the ground) is:
questions.x: Total energy = mgH = 200 J; KE = PE when each is 100 J, at a height of 10 m. Then ½ × 1 × v² = 100, so v = √200 = 10√2 m s⁻¹. 20 m s⁻¹ is its speed on reaching the ground.

questions.q: A wheel of radius 25 cm rotates so that a point on its rim moves at 5 m s⁻¹. The angular velocity of the wheel is:
questions.x: ω = v/r = 5/0.25 = 20 rad s⁻¹ (check: 0.25 × 20 = 5 m s⁻¹). Leaving the radius in centimetres gives 5/25 = 0.2 rad s⁻¹; multiplying instead of dividing gives 1.25.

questions.q: Water (density 1000 kg m⁻³) flows through a horizontal pipe whose wide part has four times the cross-sectional area of its narrow part. The speed in the wide part is 1 m s⁻¹. The pressure in the wide part exceeds that in the narrow part by:
questions.x: Continuity gives v₂ = 4 × 1 = 4 m s⁻¹. Bernoulli: P₁ − P₂ = ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²) = ½ × 1000 × (16 − 1) = 7500 Pa. Forgetting the ½ gives 15000 Pa; ignoring v₁ gives 8000 Pa; not squaring the speeds gives 1500 Pa.

questions.q: A particle performs SHM with amplitude 0.02 m and frequency 5 Hz. The magnitude of its maximum acceleration is:
questions.x: ω = 2πf = 10π rad s⁻¹ and a_max = ω²x₀ = 100π² × 0.02 = 2π² m s⁻² (about 20 m s⁻²). 0.2π m s⁻¹ is ωx₀, the maximum speed; using f² x₀ without 2π gives 0.5.

questions.q: In simple harmonic motion, the phase of the vibrating particle at an instant tells us its:
o: Maximum displacement from the mean position
Number of vibrations completed each second
Position and direction of motion at that instant
questions.x: Phase (the angle ωt + φ) fixes where the particle is in its cycle and which way it is moving at that moment. The maximum displacement is the amplitude and vibrations per second is the frequency.

questions.q: The speed of sound in a gas does NOT depend on the:
o: Ratio of specific heats γ of the gas
questions.x: v = √(γP/ρ) = √(γRT/M) contains no frequency, so all frequencies travel at the same speed (otherwise music heard from far away would arrive out of step). Temperature, molar mass and γ all change v.

questions.q: A diffraction grating is ruled with 4000 lines per centimetre. Light of wavelength 625 nm falls on it normally. What is sin θ for the first-order maximum?
questions.x: Grating element d = 1/4000 cm = 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m, so sin θ = λ/d = 625 × 10⁻⁹/2.5 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.25. Check: d/λ = 4. Treating the 4000 lines as per millimetre gives 0.025.

questions.q: A person can hear a radio playing behind a wall but cannot see it. This is mainly because:
o: The wavelength of sound is comparable to the size of the wall and doorways, while light's wavelength is far smaller
questions.x: Diffraction is large only when the obstacle or opening is comparable to the wavelength. Sound wavelengths are about a metre, light wavelengths about 5 × 10⁻⁷ m, so sound bends round the wall and light does not. Sound is longitudinal and slower than light.

questions.q: An ideal gas expands adiabatically and does 400 J of work. It is then heated at constant volume until it is back at its starting temperature. How much heat is needed?
questions.x: Adiabatic: Q = 0, so ΔU = −400 J and the gas cools. To return to the starting temperature its internal energy must rise by 400 J; at constant volume no work is done, so Q = 400 J.

questions.q: Which of these processes is closest to being reversible?
o: Heat flowing from a hot cup of tea into a cool room
A gas rushing into a vacuum
A very slow, frictionless compression of a gas, done in tiny steps
A ball bouncing on the floor until it comes to rest
questions.x: A reversible process passes through equilibrium states and can be run backwards with no lasting change, which needs a slow change with no friction. Heat flow across a temperature difference, free expansion and friction are all irreversible.

questions.q: A proton and an electron are placed in the same uniform electric field. Compared with the proton, the electron experiences:
o: A larger force in the same direction
A smaller force and a smaller acceleration
A force of the same size in the opposite direction, and a much larger acceleration
The same force and the same acceleration
questions.x: F = qE and both carry charge of size e, so the forces are equal in size but opposite in direction. The electron's mass is about 1/1836 of the proton's, so a = F/m is far larger.

questions.q: Electric field lines never cross each other because:
o: The field has only one direction at any point
The field is zero where lines meet
questions.x: The tangent to a field line gives the direction of the field. If two lines crossed, the field would have two directions at one point, which is impossible.

questions.q: Resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 6 Ω are connected in parallel across a 6 V battery of negligible internal resistance. The total current drawn from the battery is:
questions.x: 1/R = 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6 = 1, so R = 1 Ω and I = 6/1 = 6 A. Check: 3 A + 2 A + 1 A = 6 A. Adding the resistors as if in series (11 Ω) gives about 0.55 A.

questions.q: For a metal wire, resistance R is plotted against temperature θ in °C. The graph is a straight line, R = R₀(1 + αθ), where R₀ is the resistance at 0 °C. The gradient of this line equals:
questions.x: R = R₀ + (αR₀)θ, a straight line of intercept R₀ and gradient αR₀. α alone is the gradient divided by the intercept.

questions.q: A velocity selector has uniform electric and magnetic fields at right angles to each other and to a beam of particles. Which particles pass straight through undeflected?
o: Only positive particles with speed E/B
Only particles of one particular mass
Only those with speed E/B, whatever their charge or mass
questions.x: No deflection needs qE = qvB, so v = E/B; q cancels, and mass does not appear. For a negative particle both forces reverse together and still balance. Faster particles are pushed aside by the larger magnetic force.

questions.q: A wire bent into a semicircle of radius 0.1 m carries a current of 5 A. A uniform magnetic field of 0.2 T acts perpendicular to the plane of the semicircle. The resultant force on the semicircular wire is (π ≈ 3.14):
questions.x: In a uniform field a curved wire feels the same resultant force as a straight wire joining its ends, here the diameter 2r = 0.2 m: F = BIL = 0.2 × 5 × 0.2 = 0.2 N. Using the arc length πr = 0.314 m gives 0.314 N, but the sideways parts of the arc cancel.

questions.q: A flat wire loop lies in the plane of the page in a uniform magnetic field directed into the page. The field strength is increasing. Viewed from the front of the page, the induced current in the loop is:
o: Zero, because the field is uniform
questions.x: The inward flux is increasing, so by Lenz's law the induced current makes a field out of the page, inside the loop. By the right-hand grip rule that needs an anticlockwise current. Clockwise would add to the increasing inward flux.

questions.q: A sinusoidal alternating current of peak value 2 A flows through a 10 Ω resistor. The average power dissipated in the resistor is:
questions.x: P = I(rms)²R = (I₀²/2)R = (4/2) × 10 = 20 W. Using the peak current, I₀²R, gives 40 W.

questions.q: A rubber band can be stretched to several times its length and still return to its original length. This is mainly because rubber:
o: Has a regular crystal lattice whose atoms move far apart
Is an amorphous solid with no bonds between its molecules
Is made of long, coiled chain molecules that straighten when stretched and coil up again
Has a very high Young's modulus
questions.x: Rubber is a polymeric solid: its long chain molecules are tangled and coiled, so a pull mainly straightens them, and they coil back when released. A high Young's modulus would mean a stiff material that hardly stretches, the opposite of rubber.

questions.q: A transistor is used as a switch in a circuit. It acts as an open (OFF) switch when:
o: The base current is zero, so the collector current is almost zero
The base current is large, so the collector current is at its maximum
The collector-emitter voltage is almost zero
The base-emitter junction is forward biased with a large current
questions.x: With no base current the transistor is cut off: I_C ≈ 0 and almost the whole supply voltage appears across the collector and emitter, like an open switch. A large base current saturates it, with V_CE near zero, which is the ON state.

questions.q: A frame fixed to the Earth's surface is only approximately an inertial frame because:
o: The Earth's gravity pulls on bodies in the frame
Light travels more slowly near the Earth
The Earth moves at a constant velocity through space
The Earth spins on its axis and moves round the Sun, so the frame has a small acceleration
questions.x: Rotation and orbital motion give every point on the Earth a small centripetal acceleration, so strictly the frame is non-inertial, though the effects are small enough to ignore in most experiments. Motion at constant velocity would make it exactly inertial.

questions.q: Photons of energy 3 eV fall on a metal of work function 2 eV. The maximum speed of the emitted photoelectrons is about: (mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)
questions.x: K.E.max = 3 − 2 = 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, so v = √(2 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ / 9.1 × 10⁻³¹) = √(3.5 × 10¹¹) ≈ 5.9 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹. Leaving out the 2 gives 4.2 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹; using the work function 2 eV as the kinetic energy gives 8.4 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹, and using the photon energy 3 eV gives 1.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹.

questions.q: The wavelengths of the Balmer series of hydrogen are given by 1/λ = R_H (1/2² − 1/n²). In this formula n takes the values:
questions.x: Balmer lines come from electrons falling to n = 2 from higher levels, so n = 3, 4, 5, … (n = 2 would give 1/λ = 0, no line). Starting at n = 2 is the common slip; n = 4, 5, … would leave out the red line from n = 3.

questions.q: In Rutherford's experiment, most of the alpha particles fired at a thin gold foil passed straight through it. This showed that:
o: The atom's positive charge is spread evenly through it
Most of the atom is empty space
questions.x: If most alpha particles meet nothing that deflects them, the atom must be mostly empty space. The few large-angle deflections were what showed a tiny, dense, positive nucleus; an evenly spread positive charge could not produce them.

questions.q: A proton is made of three quarks. Its quark content is:
questions.x: Up quarks have charge +⅔e and down quarks −⅓e, so u u d gives ⅔ + ⅔ − ⅓ = +1e, the proton's charge. u d d gives 0 (the neutron); u u u gives +2e.

questions.q: Complete combustion of 1.5 g of an organic compound gives 2.2 g of CO₂. The percentage of carbon in the compound is: (C = 12, O = 16)
questions.x: Mass of C = 2.2 × 12/44 = 0.6 g, so %C = 0.6/1.5 × 100 = 40%. 27.3% is just the carbon fraction of CO₂ (12/44), forgetting to relate it to the sample; 60% is the remaining percentage, not the carbon.

questions.q: A crude solid is being purified by crystallisation, but its hot solution is coloured by an impurity. The colour is best removed by:
o: Adding more solvent and cooling quickly
Washing the final crystals with hot solvent
Heating the crystals until the colour disappears
Boiling the solution with a little animal charcoal and filtering it hot
questions.x: Animal charcoal adsorbs coloured impurities and is removed by hot filtration, leaving a colourless solution to crystallise. Washing with hot solvent would dissolve the product itself, and heating the crystals does not remove the impurity.

questions.q: The gas constant R = 0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. In SI units its value is:
questions.x: 1 dm³ atm = 101.3 J, so 0.0821 × 101.3 ≈ 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. 1.987 is the value in cal K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and 62.4 is in dm³ mm Hg K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, not joules.

questions.q: Two closed flasks at 25 °C contain water: one holds 10 cm³ with a small surface, the other 100 cm³ with a much larger surface. Once equilibrium is reached, the vapour pressure of water is:
o: Greater in the flask with more water
Greater in the flask with the larger surface
Greater in the flask with less water
questions.x: Equilibrium vapour pressure depends only on the liquid and its temperature. A larger surface makes evaporation and condensation both faster, so equilibrium is reached sooner but at the same pressure.

questions.q: Which order of the subshells is in increasing energy, as used for filling by the Aufbau principle?
questions.x: (n + l): 4s = 4, 3d = 5, 4p = 5, 5s = 5. 4s is lowest; among those with n + l = 5, the lower n fills first: 3d, then 4p, then 5s. Ordering by n alone puts 3d first.

questions.q: The shape of an s orbital is:
questions.x: An s orbital (l = 0) is spherically symmetrical about the nucleus. Dumbbell is the shape of a p orbital and double dumbbell describes most d orbitals.

questions.q: Which order of carbon–carbon bond length is correct?
questions.x: More shared pairs pull the two nuclei closer: C–C about 154 pm, C=C about 134 pm and C≡C about 120 pm. Bond energy runs the other way (C≡C strongest), which is why the reversed order is tempting.

questions.q: For a reaction, the activation energy of the forward reaction is 90 kJ mol⁻¹ and that of the reverse reaction is 30 kJ mol⁻¹. What is ΔH of the forward reaction?
questions.x: On the energy profile, ΔH = Ea(forward) − Ea(reverse) = 90 − 30 = +60 kJ mol⁻¹: the products lie 60 kJ above the reactants, so the reaction is endothermic. Subtracting the other way gives −60; adding the two gives 120.

questions.q: For which equilibrium is Kp = Kc(RT)²?
questions.x: Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn, where Δn = moles of gaseous products − moles of gaseous reactants. For 2NH₃ ⇌ N₂ + 3H₂, Δn = 4 − 2 = +2. The ammonia synthesis has Δn = −2 (Kp = Kc(RT)⁻²), PCl₅ has +1 and HI has 0.

questions.q: Equal volumes of hydrochloric acid of pH 2.0 and hydrochloric acid of pH 4.0 are mixed at 25 °C. What is the pH of the mixture, approximately? (log 5 = 0.70)
questions.x: [H⁺] values are 1 × 10⁻² and 1 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³; mixing equal volumes gives (0.010 + 0.0001) ÷ 2 ≈ 5.05 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³, so pH = 3 − log 5.05 ≈ 3 − 0.70 = 2.3. Averaging the two pH values gives 3.0, the tempting slip, because pH is a log scale.

questions.q: According to the Arrhenius concept, a base is a substance that:
o: Accepts a proton from another species
Gives hydroxide ions, OH⁻, when dissolved in water
Donates a pair of electrons to form a coordinate bond
Gives hydrogen ions, H⁺, when dissolved in water
questions.x: Arrhenius defined acids as giving H⁺ and bases as giving OH⁻ in aqueous solution. Accepting a proton is the Brønsted–Lowry definition and donating an electron pair is the Lewis definition, so those describe bases under the other concepts.

questions.q: The particles of a sol such as iron(III) hydroxide sol do not join together and coagulate in the pure sol mainly because:
o: All the particles carry the same kind of electric charge and repel one another
They are too small ever to collide with one another
They are present as separate dissolved ions
They are lighter than the water molecules around them
questions.x: Each colloidal particle adsorbs ions of one kind and so carries the same charge as the others; the repulsion keeps them apart. Adding an electrolyte neutralises this charge and causes coagulation.

questions.q: When a lead storage battery discharges, which substance forms on both the positive and the negative plates?
questions.x: Negative plate: Pb + SO₄²⁻ → PbSO₄ + 2e⁻. Positive plate: PbO₂ + 4H⁺ + SO₄²⁻ + 2e⁻ → PbSO₄ + 2H₂O. Both plates become coated with lead(II) sulphate; PbO₂ and Pb are the starting materials, which recharging restores.

questions.q: On a graph of reactant concentration against time, the instantaneous rate of reaction at a particular time is found from the:
o: Area under the curve up to that time
Concentration at that time divided by the time
Slope of the tangent to the curve at that time
Slope of the straight line joining the start of the curve to that point
questions.x: The instantaneous rate is −d[reactant]/dt, the gradient of the tangent at that point. The line from the start of the curve to the point gives the average rate over the interval, the usual mix-up.

questions.q: The first electron affinity of oxygen is exothermic, but adding a second electron, O⁻(g) + e⁻ → O²⁻(g), is endothermic. This is because:
o: The incoming electron is repelled by the negative charge of O⁻
The second electron enters a higher shell
Oxygen has a low nuclear charge
The O²⁻ ion is smaller than the O⁻ ion
questions.x: O⁻ is already negative, so energy must be supplied to force a second electron onto it against the repulsion. That electron still goes into the 2p subshell, and O²⁻ is larger than O⁻, not smaller.

questions.q: The solubility of Group 2 sulphates decreases from MgSO₄ to BaSO₄. The main reason is that, down the group:
o: The charge on the cation increases
The hydration energy of the cation falls faster than the lattice energy, which changes little because the sulphate ion is large
questions.x: With the large SO₄²⁻ ion, a bigger cation hardly changes the lattice energy, but the hydration energy of the cation falls steadily as it gets larger. Less energy is released on dissolving, so solubility falls. The charge stays +2 throughout.

questions.q: In a fully charged lead-acid storage battery, the active material of the positive plate and the oxidation state of lead in it are:
questions.x: The positive plate carries lead(IV) oxide, PbO₂ (Pb +4), and the negative plate spongy lead; on discharge both turn into PbSO₄. Choosing PbSO₄ describes a discharged plate, the usual slip.

questions.q: In the P₄O₁₀ molecule, each P atom is bonded to four O atoms, and the P atoms are linked through P–O–P bridges. How many oxygen atoms are in P–O–P bridges?
questions.x: P₄O₁₀ is the P₄O₆ cage (six bridging O along the six edges of the P₄ tetrahedron) plus one terminal P=O on each of the four P atoms: 6 + 4 = 10 O. Check: each P has 3 bridging + 1 terminal = 4 O. Giving the 4 terminal oxygens is the slip.

questions.q: Chlorine shows oxidation states from −1 to +7 in its compounds, but fluorine shows only −1. The best explanation is that fluorine:
o: Is the most electronegative element and has no d orbitals in its valence shell
Has the highest electron affinity of all the elements
Has a very strong F–F bond
Has the largest atomic radius in the group
questions.x: No element is more electronegative than fluorine, so it cannot take a positive state, and with only 2s and 2p orbitals it cannot expand its octet as chlorine does with 3d orbitals. Chlorine, not fluorine, has the highest electron affinity, and the F–F bond is weak, so the other options are false.

questions.q: Which of these aqueous ions is colourless?
questions.x: Colour needs a d–d transition, so at least one d electron and a vacancy. Sc³⁺ is 3d⁰ and colourless, while Ti³⁺ (3d¹), V³⁺ (3d²) and Cr³⁺ (3d³) are coloured. Counting the 4s electrons as still present for Sc³⁺ is the slip.

questions.q: Which order shows the types of coal in increasing carbon content?
questions.x: Coal forms over long periods of heat and pressure; the older and more compressed it is, the more carbon it has: peat (lowest), lignite, bituminous coal, then anthracite (about 90% or more). Writing the order backwards is the usual slip.

questions.q: Ethene is bubbled into bromine water that also contains dissolved sodium chloride. Besides BrCH₂CH₂Br, some BrCH₂CH₂Cl is formed, but no ClCH₂CH₂Cl. This shows that:
o: Both halogen atoms add to the double bond together in a single step
Bromine adds first as an electrophile, and the intermediate is then attacked by any nucleophile present, including Cl⁻
Bromine oxidises Cl⁻ to Cl₂, which then adds to ethene
Chlorine free radicals formed from NaCl attack ethene
questions.x: If both atoms added together, only BrCH₂CH₂Br could form. Every product has one Br, so Br⁺ adds first and the cation is then captured by Br⁻, Cl⁻ or water. Br₂ cannot oxidise Cl⁻, which is why no dichloro product appears.

questions.q: When benzene is alkylated with chloromethane and anhydrous AlCl₃, products with two or more methyl groups also form. The reason is that:
o: The methyl group deactivates the ring, so the reaction cannot stop
The methyl group on the product activates the ring, so methylbenzene reacts faster than benzene
AlCl₃ adds to the ring and is replaced by methyl groups
Chloromethane decomposes to give methyl free radicals
questions.x: An alkyl group donates electron density to the ring, so the first product is more reactive than the starting benzene and is alkylated again (polyalkylation). A deactivating group would do the opposite and slow further substitution.

questions.q: An optically active sample of 3-bromo-3-methylhexane, a tertiary alkyl halide, is hydrolysed by water through the SN1 mechanism. The alcohol formed is:
o: Only the isomer with inverted configuration
Only the isomer with the same configuration
Not formed, because tertiary halides do not undergo substitution
A racemic mixture, because the flat carbocation is attacked equally from both faces
questions.x: The C–Br bond breaks first to give a planar sp² carbocation; water can attack either face equally, giving both mirror-image alcohols in equal amounts. Complete inversion is the result of SN2 back-side attack.

questions.q: Ethanol reacts with sodium metal to give hydrogen, but ethoxyethane does not. The reason is that ethoxyethane:
o: Has no lone pairs on its oxygen atom
Is a stronger acid than ethanol
Has a higher boiling point than ethanol
Has no hydrogen atom bonded to oxygen
questions.x: Sodium releases H₂ only from O–H (acidic) hydrogens. In C₂H₅OC₂H₅ all hydrogens are on carbon. The ether oxygen still has two lone pairs, and ether boils lower than ethanol.

questions.q: Ethyne is passed into dilute sulphuric acid containing mercury(II) sulphate at about 75 °C. The final organic product is:
questions.x: Water adds across one π bond to give CH₂=CHOH (vinyl alcohol), which is unstable and rearranges to CH₃CHO. Ethanol would need two additions of hydrogen, not water; propanone forms from propyne, not ethyne.

questions.q: Ethanoic anhydride, (CH₃CO)₂O, is warmed with ethanol. The products are:
questions.x: (CH₃CO)₂O + C₂H₅OH → CH₃COOC₂H₅ + CH₃COOH: one acyl group goes to the alcohol and the other leaves as ethanoic acid. Writing water as the by-product mixes this up with esterification of the acid itself.

questions.q: Which two-step route converts bromoethane, CH₃CH₂Br, into propylamine, CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂?
o: Heat with ethanolic KCN, then boil the product with dilute acid
Heat with excess ammonia in a sealed tube, then reduce the product with LiAlH₄
Boil with aqueous KOH, then heat the product with ammonia
Heat with ethanolic KCN, then reduce the product with LiAlH₄ in dry ether
questions.x: KCN replaces Br by CN, adding one carbon (CH₃CH₂CN, propanenitrile), and LiAlH₄ reduces –CN to –CH₂NH₂, giving CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂. Hydrolysis with acid would give propanoic acid instead, and ammonia alone gives ethylamine, which has one carbon too few.

questions.q: A compound contains two chlorine atoms. Taking ³⁵Cl : ³⁷Cl = 3 : 1, its M, M+2 and M+4 peaks have heights in the ratio of about:
questions.x: With two Cl atoms the chances are (3/4)² for ³⁵Cl³⁵Cl, 2 × (3/4)(1/4) for one of each and (1/4)² for ³⁷Cl³⁷Cl, that is 9/16 : 6/16 : 1/16 = 9 : 6 : 1. Forgetting the factor 2 for the mixed pair gives 9 : 3 : 1; 1 : 2 : 1 is the pattern for two Br atoms.

questions.q: In nuclear fission of uranium-235:
o: A heavy nucleus absorbs a neutron and splits into two medium-sized nuclei, releasing energy and more neutrons
Two light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus
A nucleus emits an α-particle and becomes a lighter element only
Uranium atoms burn in oxygen to release heat
questions.x: U-235 captures a slow neutron and splits into two smaller nuclei plus two or three neutrons, which can carry on a chain reaction; the lost mass appears as energy. Joining light nuclei is fusion, the opposite process.

questions.q: Which statement about a compiler and an interpreter is correct?
o: A compiler translates the whole program first; an interpreter translates and runs one statement at a time
An interpreter translates the whole program first; a compiler translates and runs one statement at a time
A compiler translates assembly language only; an interpreter translates machine language only
Both translate the whole program first and differ only in the speed of the computer they need
questions.x: A compiler converts the complete source program into machine code before it runs, while an interpreter takes one statement, translates it, executes it, then moves on. The reversed statement swaps the two definitions.

questions.q: Moving down the memory hierarchy from registers to cache to RAM to hard disk, which statement is true?
o: Capacity, speed and cost per byte all increase
Capacity decreases while speed and cost per byte increase
Capacity increases while speed and cost per byte decrease
Speed increases while capacity and cost per byte decrease
questions.x: Registers are the fastest and most expensive per byte but tiny; each lower level is slower and cheaper per byte but much larger. That is why a computer has only a few registers but a disk of hundreds of gigabytes.

questions.q: Which storage device uses flash memory and has no moving parts?
questions.x: An SSD stores data in flash memory chips, so nothing spins or moves. A hard disk has spinning platters and moving heads, and tape and DVD drives also have moving parts.

questions.q: Which list puts a hub, a switch and a router in order of the OSI layer at which each mainly works, lowest layer first?
questions.x: A hub works at layer 1 (Physical), a switch at layer 2 (Data Link, using MAC addresses) and a router at layer 3 (Network, using IP addresses). Putting the router before the switch reverses layers 2 and 3.

questions.q: Which is an important advantage of fibre-optic cable over twisted-pair copper cable?
o: It is cheaper and easier to join
It carries electricity to power the computers
It carries much more data over longer distances
It can bend around very sharp corners without loss
questions.x: Light pulses in glass fibre give very high bandwidth and lose little strength over long distances. Fibre is actually more expensive and harder to join than copper, which is its main drawback.

questions.q: With the subnet mask 255.255.255.0, which address is on the same network as 192.168.4.17?
questions.x: The mask 255.255.255.0 means the first three numbers name the network, so the network is 192.168.4; only 192.168.4.200 shares it. 192.168.40.17 looks similar, but its third number is 40, not 4.

questions.q: Nida receives a chat message from her friend's account asking her to send money urgently for an emergency. What is the safest thing to do?
o: Send the money, since it came from the friend's account
Call the friend on a number she already knows to check first
Reply in the same chat asking the sender to prove who they are
Forward the message to other friends to warn them
questions.x: If the account was hacked, the attacker controls that chat and can answer any question there, so checking through a separate, known channel is safest. Sending money because the account looks familiar is exactly what the scam relies on.

questions.q: Hira writes a program and posts its code on her blog. She does not register it anywhere and writes no copyright notice. Who holds the copyright in the code?
o: Nobody, because the code was never registered
Anyone who downloads the code from the blog
The company that runs the blog website
Hira, because copyright arises automatically when a work is created
questions.x: Copyright belongs to the author from the moment an original work is created; registration and notices are optional. Posting it online does not hand the rights to readers or to the blog host.

questions.q: A hospital is unsure about putting its patient records in a public cloud. What is its main concern?
o: The data would be held on servers controlled by another company
Cloud storage cannot hold text files
Patients' records would load too slowly to read
The public cloud would delete old records every month
questions.x: In a public cloud the provider's staff and systems hold the data, so privacy and security of sensitive records are the worry. That is why such organisations often choose a private cloud.

questions.q: Five lines of text each hold 3 words separated by tabs, with no tab at the start or end of a line. The text is converted to a table using tabs as the separator. What size is the table?
questions.x: Each line becomes one row, so there are 5 rows, and the 2 tabs on each line split it into 3 cells, giving 3 columns. Counting the tabs (2) instead of the pieces they separate gives the wrong 2 columns.

questions.q: In a marks list, a filter is set to show only students with Marks greater than 50. What happens to the rows of the other students?
o: They are deleted from the worksheet
They are moved to a new worksheet
They are hidden but not deleted
questions.x: A filter only hides the rows that do not meet the condition; clearing the filter shows them again unchanged. Nothing is deleted, moved or changed.

questions.q: A list of items in no particular order, where each item starts with a small dot or other symbol, is a:
questions.x: A bulleted list marks items with symbols when order does not matter. A numbered list is used when the order of the items matters, such as steps.

questions.q: In a file-based system, the rule "marks cannot be more than 100" has to be written into every program that enters marks, and some programs forget it. Which limitation of file systems is this?
questions.x: When each program must check rules such as marks ≤ 100 by itself, the rules are hard to enforce and change, so wrong data gets in; this is the integrity problem. Program-data dependence is about programs having to change when the record layout changes.

questions.q: Tables, primary key first: Student(RollNo, SName), Dept(DeptID, DName), Course(CourseID, Title, DeptID), Teacher(TeacherID, TName, DeptID), Enrol(RollNo, CourseID, Grade) with key (RollNo, CourseID). A column with the same name as another table's primary key is a foreign key to it. How many foreign key columns are there in all?
questions.x: Course.DeptID, Teacher.DeptID, Enrol.RollNo and Enrol.CourseID refer to other tables: 4 columns. The two columns of Enrol's key are also foreign keys; missing them gives 2, and Student.RollNo is a primary key, not a foreign key.

questions.q: Which type of Access query raises the Price of every Physics book by 10% in one step?
questions.x: An update query changes the values in many existing records at once. A select query only shows records, and an append query adds records to another table.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT an object of an MS Access database?
questions.x: Access database objects include tables, queries, forms, reports, macros and modules. A slide belongs to a PowerPoint presentation, not to an Access database.

questions.x: The first scanf reads 3 and leaves " 9" waiting; the second %d skips the space and reads 9, so b - a = 9 - 3 = 6. A space separates numbers just as Enter does.
%d reads 5 into n and %f reads 2.5 into x; n * x = 12.5, printed with one decimal place. 7.5 would be n + x.
p == q is false, so the first test fails. In the second test p == r (5 == 5) is true, so isosceles is printed and the else is skipped. Only one branch of an else-if ladder runs.

first returns the smallest divisor from 2 upwards: 35 % 5 == 0 is the first hit (35 is odd and 35 % 3 = 2, 35 % 4 = 3), so 5. 13 has no divisor below 13, so the loop ends and return n gives 13. 7 is a divisor of 35 but is found after 5.

The outer loop runs 3 times (i = 0, 1, 2) and for each of them the inner loop runs 4 times (j = 0 to 3), so 3 x 4 = 12 stars. 7 adds the counts instead of multiplying; 20 wrongly counts 4 x 5 as if both ends were included.

questions.q: A project has four tasks. P takes 3 weeks and starts at once. Q takes 2 weeks and can start only after P ends. R takes 4 weeks and starts at the same time as P. S takes 1 week and can start only after both Q and R end. What is the shortest time to finish the project?
questions.x: The chain P then Q ends after 3 + 2 = 5 weeks, while R running alongside ends after 4 weeks; S must wait for the later one, so it runs in week 6 and the project takes 5 + 1 = 6 weeks. 10 weeks adds all tasks as if none ran in parallel.

questions.q: A hospital receives its new system, built with the Waterfall model, 14 months after the project began. The staff find that several screens do not match the way they actually work. Which weakness of Waterfall does this show?
o: Too many small releases confused the staff
Users see working software only near the end, so misunderstandings are found late
Testing was done before the code was written
questions.x: In Waterfall the users mostly see the system after coding and testing are complete, so a misunderstood requirement surfaces late, when it is costly to fix. Waterfall does have a requirements stage at the very start, and frequent small releases belong to Agile.

questions.q: In object-oriented programming, what is an object?
o: A function that returns a class
A keyword that defines a new data type
An instance of a class, with its own values for the class's attributes
A variable that can hold only numbers
questions.x: A class is the blueprint and each object made from it is an instance with its own attribute values. The keyword that defines a new type is `class`, not an object.

questions.q: A Tkinter form must let a student tick any number of the subjects Physics, Chemistry and Computer. Which widget suits each subject?
questions.x: Checkbuttons can be ticked independently, so any number can be chosen. Radiobuttons in a group allow only one choice at a time.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
print("Ha" * 3)
```
questions.x: `*` with a string and a whole number repeats the string: "Ha" three times, joined with nothing between, gives HaHaHa. Python does not turn the 3 into text (Ha3), and repetition adds no spaces.

questions.q: For p = T, q = F and r = T, what are the values of (p → q) ∨ ¬r and (p ∨ q) ∧ r, in that order?
questions.x: p → q is T → F = F and ¬r = F, so F ∨ F = F. p ∨ q = T and r = T, so T ∧ T = T.

questions.q: A graph in which every edge has a direction, such as a map of one-way roads, is called:
questions.x: When each edge goes one way only (from one vertex to another), the graph is directed. In an undirected graph each edge can be followed both ways.

questions.q: Which property of an algorithm requires every step to be precise and to have only one meaning?
questions.x: Definiteness means each step is clearly and unambiguously stated. Finiteness is about the algorithm stopping after a limited number of steps.

questions.q: A survey asks 300 students, chosen from all 12,000 students of a university, about their study hours. The 300 students form:
questions.x: The population is the whole group of interest (all 12,000 students); the 300 chosen from it are a sample. A control group belongs to an experiment, not a survey.

questions.q: The story told in the passage is mainly about:
o: how the narrator became the strongest player in the club
why Danish was a better player than the narrator
how school chess clubs are organised
how losing at chess taught the narrator a habit of thinking before acting
questions.x: The narrator "never became very good" but took away "the habit of stopping, before I act, to ask what I am actually hoping will happen". Becoming the strongest player is contradicted.

questions.q: What did Mehwish do after each game?
o: She laughed at the mistakes he had made
She taught him the best opening moves
She refused to play him again
She reset the position where his game had gone wrong and asked him a question
questions.x: She would "set the pieces back to where my position had fallen apart and ask" him what he had hoped for, "without a trace of mockery", so she did not laugh at him.

questions.q: The narrator's feeling that the road was "tilting downhill" suggests that he felt:
o: tired after a long and difficult game
light and happy, as if things had suddenly become easier
nervous about his next game against Danish
worried that he had taken the wrong road home
questions.x: He felt this on the day he first drew against Danish after a month of losing, so walking downhill suggests ease and lightness. Tiredness does not fit the joy of his first good result.

questions.q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "trace" most nearly means:
questions.x: Mehwish asked "without a trace of mockery", meaning with not the slightest sign of it, which fits her patient help. A drawing made by copying is another meaning of the word, not this one.

questions.q: Looking back on his time in the club, the narrator's attitude is best described as:
o: bitter about having lost so many games
proud of having become a strong player
grateful, valuing what he learned though he never played well
indifferent to the club and its members
questions.x: He says he took something "that I have used far more often than any chess opening", which shows gratitude. He admits "I never became very good", so pride in being strong is wrong.

questions.q: Which title would suit the passage best?
o: How Bees Make Honey from Nectar
The Dangers of Spraying Fruit Trees
Why Wind Is the Orchard's Best Friend
questions.x: The passage explains why owners rent hives "while the trees are in flower" and how the arrangement works. Spraying is only one condition of the deal, and wind "does little of this work".

questions.q: According to the passage, why do some large orchards need hired bees?
o: Their trees make no pollen of their own
The wind carries too much of their pollen away
Their owners want to sell honey
They have too few wild insects to visit every blossom in time
questions.x: Large orchards "often have too few wild insects to visit every blossom in the short time the trees are in flower". The honey goes to the beekeepers, not the orchard owners.

questions.q: It can be inferred that a small orchard surrounded by hedges and wild flowers:
o: needs more hired hives than a large orchard
may produce a good crop without hired hives
cannot be pollinated by insects at all
must never be sprayed at any time of year
questions.x: Large orchards lack insects because they have "few hedges or wild flowers nearby", and "Where wild insects are plentiful, an orchard may need no help". The passage warns only against spraying "while the trees are in bloom", not all year.

questions.q: As used in the first paragraph, the word "cargo" most nearly means:
questions.x: The "strange cargo" is the boxes of bees "stacked on the backs of pick-up trucks", a load being carried. The rent is paid for the bees; it is not the cargo itself.

questions.q: In the last paragraph, the phrase "the visitors" refers to:
o: the beekeepers who bring the hives
questions.x: The bees are brought in for a few weeks, and if the trees are sprayed "the visitors will die along with the pests". The pests cannot be meant, since the visitors die "along with" them.
